pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Salt Water vs Fresh Water

- **Standards — UK (KS2 Science working scientifically & Maths — gather, record, classify and present data; interpret and construct bar charts):** Children describe how Earth's water divides into salt water and fresh water and represent the amounts in different reservoirs on a graph.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-ESS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS2-2].

- **Operational details:** This is a quantitative, data-representation concept built on the earlier 'where water is found' survey. The three load-bearing facts: (1) about 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans; (2) only ~3% is fresh; (3) most of that fresh water is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, so the accessible surface fresh water in rivers and lakes is a tiny sliver. The pedagogy is to make children BUILD or read a graph (bar or pie) of reservoir amounts so the striking proportions become visible evidence, then reason about the distribution ('why is fresh water precious?'). Use nested representation: whole-Earth water → zoom into the 3% fresh → zoom again to the fraction that's liquid surface water.
bestPractices: Ground the numbers in a graph the child constructs or reads (bar/pie of reservoir volumes) so the 97/3 split is evidence, not a memorised fact.
Use nested/zoom representation: total water → the 3% fresh → the tiny liquid-surface fraction, so the scarcity of accessible fresh water is felt.
Connect to prior 'where water is found' work — name each reservoir (oceans, glaciers/ice caps, groundwater, rivers, lakes) before quantifying it.
Draw out the 'so what': most fresh water is frozen or underground, which is why usable fresh water is limited — an evidence-to-implication step.
Rehearse graph reading both ways: build a graph from data, and read proportions/comparisons off a given graph.
keyRepresentations: Bar chart or pie chart of reservoir volumes (ocean vs ice caps vs groundwater vs surface).
Nested 'zoom' diagram: all water → fresh water → liquid surface water.
The '100 drops' or beaker demonstration (97 salt : 3 fresh, of which ~<1 accessible).
A reservoir data table feeding a student-built graph.
commonMisconceptions: 'There's plenty of fresh water' — not seeing that most fresh water is locked in ice/underground.
'Fresh water mostly means rivers and lakes' — overlooking glaciers and groundwater as the largest fresh stores.
'Salt and fresh water are roughly equal' — underestimating the 97% ocean share.
'Percentages on a graph are the actual volumes' — confusing proportion with amount when reading the chart.
'Ice caps aren't fresh water' — not classifying glacial ice as fresh.

learn.summary: Children aged 10-11 learn that about 97% of Earth's water is salt water, almost all of it in the oceans, and only about 3% (more precisely about 2.5%) is fresh, and that most of the fresh water is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving only a tiny sliver as accessible surface water in rivers and lakes. The core move is to BUILD or READ a graph (bar or pie) of reservoir volumes so the striking proportions become visible evidence, then reason about why usable fresh water is precious. A nested 'zoom' representation (all water -> the 3% fresh -> the tiny liquid-surface fraction) is intended to make the scarcity concrete rather than merely stated.

activities.title: Build a reservoir graph, then zoom into the fresh-water slice
feedback: If the fresh share is overestimated, point back to the chart: the oceans take about 97 of every 100 parts, leaving only about 3 for all fresh water combined.
If a learner places most fresh water in rivers and lakes, zoom the fresh wedge again and show that ice caps/glaciers and groundwater hold the bulk, leaving surface water tiny.
If glaciers are excluded from fresh water, remind them that solid ice is still water: frozen fresh water holds most of the fresh supply.
If percentages are read as actual volumes, clarify that a slice shows a proportion (share) of the total, not a raw amount.
activities.rationale: Constructing and reading the graph is intended to turn the 97/3 split into evidence rather than a memorised fact, and the nested zoom aims to make the scarcity of accessible fresh water concrete. This matches a describe-and-graph objective for the distribution of water on Earth.
sourceClaims: ~97% of Earth's water is salt water; of the ~3% that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving a small fraction as accessible surface water.
learnerActions: Name each reservoir first (oceans, glaciers/ice caps, groundwater, rivers, lakes), then add its volume to a bar or pie chart one reservoir at a time; once all are added, notice that the ocean accounts for roughly 97% of the total (most of the pie, or a bar far taller than all the others combined).

Zoom into the thin ~3% 'fresh water' wedge so it fills the view, then divide that fresh slice again into its parts (mostly frozen ice caps/glaciers plus groundwater, with a hair-thin sliver of rivers and lakes).
Recompute or redraw the chart as reservoirs are included or excluded, so the proportions visibly change.

Separately, retell the same data as 100 water drops sorting themselves into about 97 salty and 3 fresh, and note how few of the fresh drops are actually reachable surface water (fewer than 1 of the 100).
State in your own words why accessible fresh water is limited, using the graph as your evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: The water people can actually reach (surface rivers and lakes) is a sliver of a sliver: only ~3% of all water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps/glaciers or held underground, which is why usable fresh water is precious.

activities.title: Hands-on beaker and 100-drops demonstration
feedback: If a learner expects the fresh portion to be large, have them look at the 30 ml beside the full litre.
If they forget the frozen/underground stores, point to the set-aside portion and note only a few drops remain reachable.
activities.rationale: A concrete volume demonstration is proposed to complement the graph by giving a physical sense of proportion that abstract percentages can obscure. The poured quantities (~30 ml fresh of ~1000 ml) approximately represent the commonly quoted rounded distribution (fresh water is closer to 2.5%, about 25 ml, and rivers plus lakes would be well under 1 ml). Presented as a complement, not a replacement, for the graphing objective.
sourceClaims: ~97% of Earth's water is salt water; of the ~3% that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving a small fraction as accessible surface water.
learnerActions: Fill a 1 litre container to represent all of Earth's water, then measure out about 30 ml to stand for the fresh water, leaving the remaining ~970 ml as the salty ocean share.
Set most of the fresh portion aside as 'frozen in ice caps' or 'underground', keeping only a few drops to represent the rivers and lakes we can easily use.
Describe what each quantity represents and compare the reachable sliver with the whole container.
Optionally re-tell the same split as 100 drops: about 97 salty, about 3 fresh, and fewer than 1 easily accessible.
activities.intendedInsight: A physical pour-off is intended to make the 97/3 proportion and the even smaller accessible fraction tangible, reinforcing the graph evidence.

activities.title: Read and reason from a supplied chart
feedback: Correct answer to the friend prompt: the friend is wrong; about 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water and only about 3% is fresh, most of which is frozen in glaciers/ice caps or stored underground, so only a tiny fraction sits in reachable rivers and lakes.
If a learner agrees with the friend, confront the ~97/3 split directly (e.g. 97 of 100 cups salty) and graph it.
If they locate the bulk of fresh water in rivers and lakes, show that ice caps/glaciers and groundwater hold most of it.

Probe deeper: 'Of 100 cups of all Earth's water, how many are salty and how many fresh?'; 'Of the fresh cups, where is most of it?'; 'The oceans look huge, but the water is salty—why does that matter for people?' (people need fresh water to drink and most crops need it to grow; salt water is not safe to drink or suitable for most farming unless it is desalinated, which is costly); 'Antarctica has almost no rivers. Could it still hold a lot of Earth's fresh water? How?' (yes, as glacial ice).
activities.rationale: Reading proportions off a supplied chart and defending an inference exercises the describe side of the objective and surfaces common misconceptions for discussion. Interpreting a given graph complements building one.
sourceClaims: ~97% of Earth's water is salt water; of the ~3% that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving a small fraction as accessible surface water.
learnerActions: Given a pie or bar chart of reservoir volumes, estimate what percentage of Earth's water is fresh.
Order the reservoirs from largest to smallest by volume.
Match each reservoir (oceans, ice caps/glaciers, groundwater, rivers, lakes) to whether the chart counts it as salt or fresh water, noting that some lakes and some groundwater are actually salty.

From the chart, state where most fresh water is stored and explain the reasoning (teaching note: the largest single fresh store is frozen ice caps/glaciers, with groundwater the next-largest; very little is in surface rivers/lakes).
Respond to the prompt: 'A friend says most of the water on Earth is fresh water we can drink. Is that right?' Explain the actual amounts and where most of Earth's water sits.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can interpret proportions and comparisons from a given graph and connect them to the real distribution of Earth's water, surfacing both the salt/fresh proportion error and the belief that visible surface water holds most fresh water.

activities.title: Motivating scaled-volume hook
feedback: Use the surprise of the small sphere to prompt the question 'and how much of that is fresh and reachable?', then hand off to the chart for the numbers.
activities.rationale: A striking scaled visual is proposed as an engaging hook; the quantitative graphing remains the mechanism for meeting the objective, so this is framed as an intro rather than the main teaching tool. Efficacy as a hook is untested and not supported by the sources, so no source claim is cited here.
learnerActions: Look at a scaled visual such as all of Earth's water gathered into a single small sphere beside the globe, or stacked water tanks scaled to reservoir volumes.
Predict how big the fresh-water portion would be before revealing it.
Move on to building or reading the actual chart to quantify the proportions.
activities.intendedInsight: A dramatic scaled-volume image may spark curiosity about how little of Earth is water we can use, motivating the graphing work that quantifies it.

constraints: Ground the numbers in a graph the child constructs or reads so the 97/3 split is treated as evidence, not a memorised fact.

Name each reservoir (oceans, glaciers/ice caps, groundwater, rivers, lakes) and classify it as salt or fresh before quantifying it, noting that the classification depends on the data set used: some lakes (e.g. the Caspian Sea, Great Salt Lake) and much deep groundwater are salty, so use the fresh-water figures given in the data; connect to prior 'where is water found?' work.
Draw out the implication: most fresh water is frozen or underground, which is why usable fresh water is limited.
Rehearse graph work both ways: build a graph from data and read proportions/comparisons off a given graph.
Scaled 3D visuals (water sphere, stacked tanks) are motivating hooks, not substitutes for the graphing that the objective requires.
A static tap-to-reveal infographic can convey the proportions and vocabulary but does not let the child assemble the graph from data, so pair it with a build-your-own-graph task when possible.
When comparing share versus amount, be explicit that a chart slice shows a proportion of the total, not a raw volume.

Treat solid ice as water: glacial ice and ice caps are frozen fresh water and must be counted when tallying fresh supplies; groundwater is also a large fresh store, so do not reduce 'most fresh water' to ice alone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two listed sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row.
Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no claim of tested effectiveness is made.

The ~97/3 figures and the 'most fresh water is frozen/underground' claim rest on the USGS source as cited; exact percentages for surface water vary by source, so treat '~3% fresh' and 'less than 1% easily accessible' as approximate.

Within the fresh ~3%, glaciers/ice caps are the largest single share and groundwater the next-largest; 'most fresh water is stored as ice' is a defensible simplification but should be taught alongside groundwater, not as the only fresh location.

A conversation/dialogue format was judged a poor fit in the source for this quantitative objective; it is omitted as a standalone activity because the payload is graph evidence, but dialogue could still support discussion of the 'so what' question without implying it is inferior for all purposes.

probeDeeper: If you filled 100 cups with all Earth's water, about how many would be salty and how many fresh?
Of the fresh-water cups, where is most of it — rivers, or ice and underground?
The oceans look huge, but the water is salty. Why does that matter for people?
Antarctica has almost no rivers. Could it still hold a lot of Earth's fresh water? How?
assess.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong. About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water; only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps or stored underground — so only a tiny fraction is in the rivers and lakes we can easily use.

errorPatterns.pattern: Most of Earth's water is fresh / drinkable ('there's water everywhere, so most is drinkable')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the ~97/3 split; graph it, e.g. 97 of 100 cups salty.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — most of Earth's water is fresh water we can drink.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees with the friend, or says fresh water is the majority.

errorPatterns.pattern: Most fresh water is in rivers and lakes (ignores glaciers and groundwater)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that most fresh water is frozen in ice caps/glaciers or held underground, not in surface rivers.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — but most of the fresh water is in the rivers and lakes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates the bulk of fresh water in the visible rivers and lakes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ice and glaciers don't count as water because they're solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Solid ice is still water — it's frozen fresh water and holds most of the fresh supply.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes glaciers/ice caps when tallying up fresh water.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks most water is fresh or drinkable; no sense of the proportions.
responseLevels.full: States the ~97% salt / ~3% fresh split AND that most fresh water is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving little accessible — and can read or sketch a graph of the reservoirs.
responseLevels.partial: Knows most water is salty (~97/3) but places most fresh water in rivers/lakes, or can't say where fresh water is stored.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Earth looks blue and covered in water from space. A friend says most of the water on Earth is fresh water we can drink. Is that right? Explain what the amounts actually are and where most of Earth's water is.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has seen a blue globe assumes 'lots of water = lots of drinkable water'. The reason tier makes them state the proportions AND where fresh water actually sits — catching both the salt/fresh proportion error and the belief that visible surface water is where most fresh water is.

sources.claim: ~97% of Earth's water is salt water; of the ~3% that is fresh, most is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving a small fraction as accessible surface water.
